alternatives.distinctnessRationale: The options differ by four courses (30 EC) in each direction. Energy systems, materials & intelligent automation adds renewable-energy resource assessment, system design, climate context and material-recovery experiments. Robotics, modelling & intelligent control adds discrete reasoning, advanced algorithms, statistical learning and AI ethics. Their shared physical, product-design and mathematical-control foundation supports mechanical-systems questions; their different priorities and methods establish distinct programmes.

Description-onlyfullsupportconsidered,notrejectedforlackofoutlines. No third standalonephysical-engineeringprogramme manufactured. Closestpriorityreassessed:energy/materialsvariantoffersstrongerphysicalbreadth,sofirst;robotics/softwaredepthsecond. Bothretainactualphysicalfoundations. comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both establish calculus used in quantitative engineering models; UCR also includes matrices and differential equations but is not mechanical-engineering mathematics.
Both use numerical methods to solve engineering-relevant equations; the external course applies them specifically to fluids and solids, which UCR does not reproduce.
Both develop probability and statistical reasoning for quantitative engineering analysis.
Both study signals and linear-system representations; UCR supplies the mathematical system framework without the surrounding mechanical laboratories.
Both include programming and computational problem solving; the external component also teaches mechanical design principles that UCR programming does not reproduce.
Both engage robotic systems; UCR teaches computational kinematics, planning and manipulation, while the external challenge integrates mechanical construction and engineering practice.
Partial ethical-reasoning correspondence through responsibility, privacy, fairness and moral frameworks applied to AI. The engineering-ethics curriculum is broader.

Partial design-project correspondence: customer needs, quantitative product models, production planning and prototypes where feasible. UCR is consumer-product development, not the full advanced mechanical-design project.
Partial physical-mechanics foundation: mechanical principles, material strength and elasticity measurements and modelling. This does not cover the full engineering mechanics course.
Partial materials correspondence through microscopic structure, macroscopic stress/strain, Mohr-circle methods and laboratory observation. Scope and engineering depth differ.

Partial technology-and-society correspondence: climate impacts, justice, energy pathways, stakeholder interviewing and public communication. The ITEC engineering-and-society curriculum has wider purposes.
Both address sustainable energy choices; UCR evaluates renewable-system designs, while the external challenge develops mechanical-engineering decisions around sustainable fuels.

Partial energy-systems correspondence: conversion, storage, resource calculations, experiments and mini-grid design. UCR does not reproduce the complete mechanical energy-storage-and-transport challenge.
Consumer Product Design does not reproduce the truss-structure mechanics and CBL integration of this component.
Differential-equation and kinematic models provide related tools, but do not establish the full mechanical-dynamics component.
Consumer-product and robotics work develops related design skills, but no launching-mechanism design-and-build project is established.
Energy-resource, hydropower and introductory physical studies provide related tools; a sufficiently specific transport-phenomena sequence is not established.
Gateway thermodynamic principles and energy-conversion study provide relevant introductory context; they do not establish a full engineering thermodynamics course.
Linear Systems and Robotics provide actual feedback, stability and motion methods, linked elsewhere. They do not reproduce the complete dynamics and control of mechanical plants.
The physical foundation includes stress/strain and Mohr-circle analysis, but does not establish the full solid-mechanics component.
Robot-arm programming, kinematics and feedback methods contribute related practice; a flexible-robot control engineering laboratory is not established.
Team product, energy and robotics projects provide some multidisciplinary practice, but not a single corresponding engineering challenge.
Introductory thermodynamic and energy-system methods do not establish the required heat-transfer and fluid-flow engineering course.
The genuine 20-EC free-elective space remains open and is not equated with scheduled UCR courses.
Material characterisation and recovery laboratories provide related experimental skills; they do not establish precision fabrication or micromanufacturing methods.
The compulsory 10-EC Mechanical Engineering final project is not a scheduled UCR course; optional UCR independent research is comparison-only.
The genuine 25-EC free-elective space remains open and is not equated with scheduled UCR courses.
Consumer-product design offers related design decisions, but no sufficiently specific precision-mechanical-engineering counterpart is established.

notes.text: The UCR options provide related study in physical and materials foundations, mathematical models, robot motion, intelligent systems, product development and sustainable energy. They differ from TU/e’s full mechanics, thermodynamics, heat and fluid flow, solid mechanics, precision manufacturing, integrated engineering laboratories and Mechanical Engineering final project.

audience.programmeDescription: TU Eindhoven Mechanical Engineering studies how physical principles, materials, mathematical models and design are used to build and control machines and energy systems. The English-taught degree combines engineering courses with team challenges and a final project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options offer related study in energy, materials and intelligent systems, or robotics and mathematical control. They include physical foundations and product work, while differing from TU/e’s sustained thermofluids, solid mechanics, precision manufacturing, engineering laboratories and compulsory Mechanical Engineering final project.

curriculum.limitation: Two core electives are selected from the approved list: Design Principles for Precision ME and Mechanical Design Project. Free electives and the final project remain subject to approval, prior preparation and availability.

componentNotes.4WC00: The required final project is 10 EC. Entry requires at least 120 EC and all compulsory first-year components before the relevant registration deadline. It can run alongside other study across two quarters or as a single-quarter block.
componentNotes.4CC50: One representative 5-EC core elective is shown. Students choose two courses from the approved eight-course list; the alternatives are not all compulsory.
componentNotes.4CBLC30: The second representative 5-EC core elective is shown here, separate from the optional precision summer-school project.
componentNotes.cp-000267-y2-open-8: 20 EC of free study in year 2, within 45 EC overall. At least 30 EC must be intermediate or advanced, including 15 EC advanced. Approval and non-overlap rules apply.
componentNotes.cp-000267-y3-open-6: 25 EC of free study in year 3 completes the 45-EC elective space.
componentNotes.0LVX10: Professional development is embedded in credited courses. Seven MyFuture points, five Studium Generale activities and required safety, computer and CANS training add no credits.
componentNotes.4CBLW00: Entry requires completion of the preceding study components embedding communication, collaboration, planning and organising competencies, insofar as they were offered in years 1 and 2.
